title: Blood bike donated in teen's memory helps save lives

input.lead: After Maisie Almond's death at 14, her family raised funds for a blood bike in her memory
input.summary: After Maisie Almond's death at 14, her family raised funds for a blood bike in her memory
input.evidence_text: Blood bike donated in teen's memory helps save lives - BBC News Image source, Family handout Image caption, Maisie Almond, from Stalybridge, was 14 when she died of liver failure. By Anna Jameson North West Published 1 hour ago The parents of a Stalybridge teenager who died while waiting for a liver transplant said a blood bike donated in her memory has helped save lives. Maisie Almond was 14 when she died of liver failure in 2024, two weeks after first complaining of a stomach ache. Despite being matched with a donor, she became too ill for a transplant to go ahead. Her family have since set up Maisie Moo's Missions in her memory and raised enough money to donate a motorbike to Greater Manchester Blood Bikes. Kathryn said: "It's something we'll never come to terms with. We're just so sad that she's been robbed of her life when she could have done so much good. We've been robbed of seeing her achieve everything she wanted to." Stuart said the family wanted to create a positive legacy in Maisie's memory. "Maisie would have needed a lot of blood for a liver transplant, so after her death we decided we wanted to do something that would help save people's lives," he said. Image caption, Maisie's parents, Stuart and Kathryn Almond, with the Maisie Moo's Missions blood bike The motorbike has joined Greater Manchester Blood Bikes' fleet of 15 vehicles and covered 600 miles in its first week alone. Dave Parsons, from Greater Manchester Blood Bikes, said: "One of the things we have to do is continually replace the motorcycles because the fleet turns over very quickly and they do a lot of miles. title: Warning to drivers as part of M60 to shut for gantries demolition

input.lead: Severe congestion is expected while work takes place at Simister Island on the M60 in Bury
input.summary: Severe congestion is expected while work takes place at Simister Island on the M60 in Bury
input.evidence_text: Warning to drivers as part of M60 to shut for gantries demolition - BBC News Image source, Google Image caption, Two gantries are being removed at Simister Island Interchange on the M60 in Bury By Lynette Horsburgh North West Published 1 hour ago Drivers are being warned of "severe congestion" when a busy stretch of motorway is closed this weekend as part of an upgrade to the road. Junction 17 and 18 of the M60 in Bury, Greater Manchester, will be shut on Saturday evening until 06:00 on Monday. The closures are to enable the demolition of two large overhead gantries at the Simister Island Interchange. It comes after two others were removed last month. National Highways said the work was part of a £300m improvement scheme and would improve traffic flow, support future housing, employment and growth across the region. Frances Oliver, of National Highways, told BBC North West Tonight : "These gantries are up to 120 tonnes so it's very similar to removing a small footbridge so it is quite a large amount of work for us to undertake." Image caption, Two busy junctions at Simister and Prestwich will be closed for the work Oliver added: "We are expecting there to be severe congestion in the area so we are asking people to plan their journeys, check before they travel and if at all try not to travel or defer their journey. "The message is if you don't need to be in the area please try not to be." input.evidence_text: Witches & Healers: Something That Was Ours - Manchester’s Finest Witches & Healers: Something That Was Ours Fri 9th Oct, 2026 - The Portico Library Witches & Healers: Something That Was Ours The Portico Library, 57 Mosley St, Manchester M2 3HY Fri 9th Oct, 2026 Free More info Directions events Go to Manchester's Finest Facebook page Go to Manchester's Finest X profile A new exhibition lands at Portico Library just in time for spooky season. Witches and Healers draws on Rosie Reed Hillman’s groundbreaking project Something That Was Ours and explores what it means to be a witch today. Themes explored include wellbeing, aging and place in relation to magic, healing and ritual offering an unparalleled insight into the diverse lives of women who live as witches and healers. Through a feminist lens Hillman uses a mixture of moving image and photography to explore menopause, mental health, outsider identities and sisterhood as well as how women imagine a better world through ritual and magic. Completely free to attend and running until February 2027, drop by to see the exhibition or book in for one of the accompanying workshops or film screenings throughout its run. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
